sa-01.exam.tasks.0.desc: Print the product name (alias product), its category (alias category) and price for products above 500.
sa-01.exam.tasks.0.title: Premium electronics with category
sa-01.lessons.0.blocks.0.html: The data is deliberately spread across tables without repetition (this is called normalisation — the 1NF/2NF/3NF topics from Week 3). products holds only a category_id, while the category name lives in categories.
sa-01.lessons.0.blocks.1.html: JOIN puts the tables back together on a condition — usually “foreign key = primary key”:
sa-01.lessons.0.blocks.3.html: Note the table aliases (p, c) — with them the query is shorter and easier to read. ON is the join condition.
sa-01.lessons.0.title: Why JOINs exist
sa-01.lessons.1.blocks.0.html: INNER JOIN (or simply JOIN) keeps only the rows that found a match in the other table:
sa-01.lessons.1.blocks.2.html: How to read it: FROM the first table → JOIN the second → ON how to connect them → then the usual WHERE/ORDER BY. A single query may contain any number of JOINs.
sa-01.lessons.1.title: INNER JOIN — matches only
sa-01.lessons.2.blocks.0.html: LEFT JOIN keeps ALL rows of the left table. Where there is no match on the right you get NULL. The classic case: “customers with no orders”:
sa-01.lessons.2.blocks.2.html: There is also RIGHT JOIN (the mirror image) and FULL JOIN (all rows of both tables) — SQL Server has both; in the trainer RIGHT/FULL are replaced by swapping the tables in a LEFT JOIN.
sa-01.lessons.2.title: LEFT JOIN — everything on the left
sa-01.lessons.3.blocks.0.html: A table can be joined to itself — that is how “an employee and their manager” is solved (the manager is a row of employees too):
sa-01.lessons.3.blocks.2.html: The trick is two different aliases for one table (e and m). The LEFT JOIN is needed so the director (who has no manager) does not disappear. This is an interview favourite!
sa-01.lessons.3.title: Self-join — a table with itself
sa-01.lessons.4.blocks.0.html: Real reports chain several tables together. “What was bought in each order”:
sa-01.lessons.4.blocks.2.html: Every JOIN adds a table to the chain through its own key. Almost every working query a Data Engineer writes looks like this — practise it until it is automatic.
sa-01.lessons.4.title: JOIN chains: 3+ tables
sa-01.quiz.0.explain: INNER JOIN keeps only the matches on the ON condition.
sa-01.quiz.0.options.0: Takes all rows of both tables
sa-01.quiz.0.options.1: Only the rows that matched the ON condition
sa-01.quiz.0.options.2: All rows of the left table
sa-01.quiz.1.explain: LEFT JOIN keeps the left row and fills the right side with NULL.
sa-01.quiz.1.q: What appears in the right table's columns in a LEFT JOIN with no match?
sa-01.quiz.2.explain: ON says which columns the tables are joined by, usually FK = PK.
sa-01.quiz.2.options.1: The condition for joining the tables
sa-01.quiz.2.q: What is ON written for in a JOIN?
sa-01.quiz.3.explain: LEFT JOIN keeps every customer, and for those without orders the order columns are NULL — that is what you catch.
sa-01.quiz.3.options.1: LEFT JOIN + WHERE o.id IS NULL
sa-01.quiz.3.q: How do you find customers WITHOUT orders?
sa-01.quiz.4.explain: One table under two aliases — that is how an employee is linked to their manager.
sa-01.quiz.4.options.1: Joining a table to itself through two aliases
sa-01.quiz.5.explain: The normal forms (1NF, 2NF, 3NF) are rules for designing tables without repeated data.
sa-01.quiz.5.options.1: Splitting data across tables without duplication
sa-01.tagline: INNER, LEFT, self-joins and table relationships · Week 3

sa-01.tasks.2.hint: FROM employees AS e LEFT JOIN employees AS m ON e.manager_id = m.id

sa-02.exam.tasks.0.desc: For every customer who has orders, print the name (alias customer) and the number of their orders (alias orders_cnt). Use JOIN and GROUP BY.
sa-02.exam.tasks.0.title: Orders per customer
sa-02.lessons.0.blocks.0.html: Aggregates collapse many rows into a single number:
sa-02.lessons.0.blocks.1.html:
• COUNT(*) — the number of rows
  • SUM(x) — the sum
  • AVG(x) — the average
  • MIN(x) / MAX(x) — minimum and maximum
sa-02.lessons.0.blocks.3.html: Important: COUNT(column) skips NULLs, while COUNT(*) counts every row.
sa-02.lessons.0.title: Aggregate functions
sa-02.lessons.1.blocks.0.html: GROUP BY splits rows into groups and applies the aggregates to each group separately. “How many customers per country”:
sa-02.lessons.1.blocks.2.html: An iron rule: SELECT may contain only columns from GROUP BY and aggregates. Anything else is an error (SQL Server will say so outright).
sa-02.lessons.1.title: GROUP BY — collapsing into groups
sa-02.lessons.2.blocks.0.html: WHERE filters rows BEFORE grouping, HAVING filters groups AFTER. The WHERE vs HAVING difference comes up in every interview (and has its own Week 2 video):
sa-02.lessons.2.blocks.2.html: The execution order of a query: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY. That is exactly why aggregates cannot appear in WHERE — the groups do not exist yet.
sa-02.lessons.2.title: HAVING — filtering groups
sa-02.lessons.3.blocks.0.html: A subquery is a query inside a query, in brackets. “Products above the average price”:
sa-02.lessons.3.blocks.2.html: A subquery can also return a list — then it is used with IN. “Customers who have orders”:
sa-02.lessons.3.blocks.4.html: A correlated subquery refers to a row of the outer query and runs once per row — the subject of its own Week 2 video. It can often be replaced by a JOIN (which is faster — the Week 3 performance topic).
sa-02.lessons.3.title: Subqueries
sa-02.lessons.4.blocks.0.html: The real power is joining tables and then collapsing them. “Revenue per order”:
sa-02.lessons.4.blocks.2.html: Queries like this are a Data Engineer's daily work: data marts, reports, metrics. Master the JOIN + GROUP BY + HAVING combination and half the job is within reach.
sa-02.lessons.4.title: JOIN + GROUP BY = a report
sa-02.quiz.0.explain: COUNT(*) counts the rows of the table (or the group).
sa-02.quiz.0.options.1: The number of rows in products
sa-02.quiz.0.q: What does SELECT COUNT(*) FROM products return?
sa-02.quiz.1.explain: The order is FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING. Aggregates can only be filtered in HAVING.
sa-02.quiz.1.options.1: WHERE filters rows before grouping, HAVING filters groups after
sa-02.quiz.1.q: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING?
sa-02.quiz.2.explain: Columns from GROUP BY plus aggregate functions. Anything else is an error.
sa-02.quiz.2.q: What may appear in SELECT with GROUP BY country?
sa-02.quiz.3.explain: COUNT(column) skips NULLs. Only COUNT(*) counts every row.
sa-02.quiz.3.q: Does COUNT(manager_id) count rows with NULL?
sa-02.quiz.4.explain: The subquery is evaluated and its result (a number) is placed into the comparison.
sa-02.quiz.4.options.1: Inside the brackets; its result is substituted into the condition
sa-02.quiz.4.q: Where does the subquery in WHERE price > (SELECT AVG(price)…) run?
sa-02.quiz.5.explain: It uses values from the outer query's current row and runs once per row.
sa-02.quiz.5.options.1: A subquery that refers to a row of the outer query

sa-03.lessons.0.blocks.0.html: WITH name AS (query) creates a temporary named result — a CTE (Common Table Expression). It is a way to break a complex query into understandable steps:
sa-03.lessons.0.blocks.2.html: First we compute the order totals (the CTE), then filter the result like an ordinary table. The mentor's Week 4 compares CTEs with temporary tables (#temp) and table variables (@table) — a CTE lives only inside a single query.
sa-03.lessons.0.title: CTE — common table expression
sa-03.lessons.1.blocks.0.html: Window functions are like aggregates but they do NOT collapse rows: every row stays and a computation “over the window” appears beside it. The keyword is OVER:
sa-03.lessons.1.blocks.2.html: PARTITION BY city splits the rows into windows per city — and each employee sees the average of THEIR city. GROUP BY would squash everything into one row per city, while a window keeps the detail. This is the number one SQL interview topic!
sa-03.lessons.1.title: Window functions: OVER
sa-03.lessons.2.blocks.0.html: Numbering functions order the rows within a window:
sa-03.lessons.2.blocks.2.html: The difference shows up on equal values: ROW_NUMBER is always 1,2,3…; RANK gives ties the same place and leaves a gap after (1,2,2,4); DENSE_RANK leaves no gaps (1,2,2,3). The question about their difference is an interview standard (and its own Week 4 video).
sa-03.lessons.2.title: ROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK
sa-03.lessons.3.blocks.0.html: LAG(x) is the value from the previous row of the window, LEAD(x) from the next one. This is how you compare “with the previous period”:
sa-03.lessons.3.blocks.2.html: A typical work task: “how much did sales grow compared with last month” — that is LAG. Without window functions you would have to write a complicated self-join.
sa-03.lessons.3.title: LAG and LEAD — neighbouring rows
sa-03.lessons.4.blocks.0.html: An aggregate plus OVER (ORDER BY …) gives a running total. A reporting classic:
sa-03.lessons.4.blocks.2.html: This is the final topic of the Week 4 programme: CTEs and window functions together. After this module you are ready for SQL Practice Problems and real SQL interviews. 🎓
sa-03.lessons.4.title: Running totals
sa-03.quiz.0.explain: WITH name AS (…) is a temporary result that lives only in this query.
sa-03.quiz.0.options.1: A named temporary result inside a query (WITH … AS)
sa-03.quiz.1.explain: GROUP BY folds a group into one row; OVER adds a computation to each row.
sa-03.quiz.1.options.1: A window does not collapse rows — every row stays
sa-03.quiz.1.q: How does a window function differ from GROUP BY?
sa-03.quiz.2.explain: RANK gives ties the same place and skips the next one: 1, 2, 2, 4.
sa-03.quiz.2.q: Prices: 100, 90, 90, 80. What does RANK() give in descending order?
sa-03.quiz.3.q: And DENSE_RANK on the same data?
sa-03.quiz.4.explain: The first row has no predecessor — LAG returns NULL (or a default if you supply one).
sa-03.quiz.4.q: What does LAG(price) return for the first row of a window?
sa-03.quiz.5.explain: PARTITION BY means “split into window groups”: the computation runs separately inside each window.
sa-03.quiz.5.options.1: Splits the rows into independent windows
sa-03.quiz.5.q: What does PARTITION BY do inside OVER?
sa-03.tasks.0.desc: Using a CTE named totals, compute the total of each order from order_items (columns order_id and total = SUM(qty*unit_price)), then print the order_id and total of orders above 900.
sa-03.tasks.0.hint: Inside the CTE: SELECT order_id, SUM(qty * unit_price) AS total FROM order_items GROUP BY order_id. Outside: WHERE total > 900.

sa-03.tasks.2.desc: Print name, salary and the employee's place by salary from highest to lowest with no gaps in the places (alias place, DENSE_RANK).
